title: Push Pull 3 days Program review
summary: He reviews a 3-day upper-body push/pull routine from a 19-year-old subscriber with cerebral palsy who has a nagging shoulder. He suggests swapping one horizontal press day for submaximal overhead pressing supersetted with face pulls, adding upper-back pulls, replacing the static 5x8 with evolving schemes, and doing long-head triceps and mid/lower trap work.
claims: A lifter training despite cerebral palsy is inspiring; fully functional people should stop making excuses
Rotating lifts can work around a shoulder problem, but the underlying issue must be fixed; a persistent ache means some lifts disagree with you or volume and intensity are wrong
Decline bench and weighted dips are very taxing on the shoulder; incline bench is less so
Vertical and horizontal pulls are different movement patterns and should not be swapped as variations of each other
His arms also started at 10 inches flexed
Strength work alone is fine early on, but later accessories and variations give you more freedom to manipulate volume and tonnage and avoid plateaus
The right weekly frequency depends on the program type: 3 days works for some programs but not for a body part split, and PPL fits poorly into 7 days
Most shoulder problems come from frequent horizontal pressing, which is prone to overuse injury
Vertical presses are among the best things you can do for shoulder health
Replace one horizontal press day with submaximal seated overhead press for 4x8-12, each set supersetted with face pulls, to bulletproof the shoulders
A shoulder that hurts at 19 only gets worse; he was lucky his problem was nerve-related, whereas a torn rotator cuff can end barbell pressing for good
Weighted chins and plate-loaded rows do not train the upper back and scapular girdle that protect the shoulders; pulling as much as you press is too simplistic because the type of pull matters
Use a high-pulling grip on rows to target the upper back, traps and rear delts
When shoulder problems piled on top of his knee problems it put him in a dark place
5x8 is worse than 5x5: if you can get 8 reps on the first of five sets you are undershooting the intensity you could reach
Prefer 5x6-10 so you experience both ends of the volume curve; reaching 5x10 guarantees you can add weight and hit 5x6
Five working sets is more than you need, in his view
Alternatively do 3 sets of 4-8 as evolving sets followed by two fixed back-off sets of 8
Static 5x8 keeps tonnage too stable, then adding weight makes it jump too suddenly, leading to plateaus or regression
5x5 is acceptable for once-weekly isolation work; do skull crushers for the long head because pressing already covers the lateral and medial heads
Frequency is your ally for growing a lagging body part; add extra arm isolation after rows and bench
His side projects are technical and fun, tax tendons more than muscle, and are kept from interfering with the program
Off days are for mental and physical recovery; leave chest, shoulders and upper back alone on them
Traps extend down the upper back; developing mid and lower traps improves posture and gives the shoulders support to tuck back when pressing
exercises: targets upper back, traps, rear delts
